messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Post-stratify and Multiplier
messages.body_plain:
Dear Camilo, listfolk,

To your first question, at present mrds/Distance doesn't offer this kind
of post-stratification, though it is something I am actively working on
at the moment. An example of the kind of stratification currently
offered in mrds (via it's simpler Distance package interface) is
available at http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.html

To your second question, multipliers are possible by modifying the
effort attached to each transect. For information on setting up your
data, you may want to look at the ?flatfile manual page in the Distance
package for how to set up your data.

Hope this helps!

best,
--dave

messages.subject: Distance 7 Release
messages.body_plain:
We would like to announce the release of Distance 7 Alpha.

With thanks to the Living Marine Resources Program for funding the development of Distance 7.

Living Marine Resource Program, US Navy,
Chief of Naval Operations, Energy and Environmental Readiness Division
N45, grant number N00244-10-1-0057

We would like to stress this is an alpha release, which means essentially that we are looking for guinea pigs.

The exciting additions to Distance 7 include the multi-analysis engine and the simulation engine. The multi-analysis engine allows you to incorporate unidentified sightings, covariate uncertainty and model uncertainty into your analyses. I am very keen to hear from anyone planning to use this functionality. The simulation engine allows you to test different designs for your specific study area and population of interest. Currently some of the more advanced options are not yet enabled in the interface but we will be working towards implementing these in the near future.

In addition we have updated the R library versions of mrds and dsm to the latest available and improved the display of R warnings to the user in the interface.

Please note that this version can happily be installed along side 6.2 (or older versions) and your distance files will NOT automatically be associated with version 7. On opening projects in version 7 you will be offered the opportunity to upgrade. Saving the upgraded project under a new name is advisable.

You will find a link to the installation at the following web address:

http://distancesampling.org/Distance/distance70download.html

Any issues can be reported via our issue tracker:

https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/distance-bugs/issues

Many thanks,

Laura

Dr. L. Marshall
Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St. Andrews

messages.subject: Second notice: distance sampling workshops, August 2015, St. Andrews
messages.subject_clean: Second notice: distance sampling workshops, August 2015, St. Andrews
messages.body_plain:
The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM) is hosting two linked workshops in the summer of 2015 in our purpose-built facilities at the University of St. Andrews, Scotland. The aim of these workshops is to train participants in the latest methods for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys, including line and point transects. The workshops are taught by leading researchers in the field, using industry-standard software.

The first workshop (11-14 August) will run at an introductory level, and will focus on distance sampling methods, largely described in the standard reference book "Introduction to Distance Sampling." The workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and participants will learn how to use the program "Distance." Participants will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and methods of analysis for distance sampling surveys.  Note that we have moved the 'automated survey design' and 'incorporating covariates in detection function' from the advanced workshop into the introductory workshop.

The advanced distance sampling workshop (17-20 August) will include advanced treatment of:  analyses in which detectability on the transect line is not assumed to be perfect (the so-called g(0) problem) and spatial (or  density surface) modelling. We will showcase a series of new R packages we have developed for performing standard as well as sophisticated analyses in R. The aim of this workshop is to bring participants up to date with the latest developments in distance sampling methods and software. It is also an opportunity for those actively engaged in the design, analysis and execution of distance sampling surveys to discuss common issues and problems, and set future research directions. The workshop will be a combination of lectures and computer sessions, with considerable time for discussion.

For all workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data sets, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.  Computer sessions take place in our modern computer classroom (attached to the seminar room); participants can use our computers or bring their own laptops.

 Additional details regarding the workshop can be found at our website
http://creem2.st-andrews.ac.uk/workshops/distance-sampling-workshops-st-andrews-august-2015/
 <http://creem2.st-andrews.ac.uk/workshops/distance-sampling-workshops-st-andrews-august-2015/>
--

I have a question similar to the one posted by Cleve Hicks on setting up data filters.  I have a field in my observation layer that refers the type of detection: visual, "a", and aural detections in three categories "b", "c", and "d" I would like run an analysis on just "a", "b", "c", by excluding category "d."  Could someone help me with syntax for this?

Caroline

All Observations

12                              b
20                              b
10                              c
2                                d
5                                d

Data filtered for type a, b, and c

0                                a
12                              b
20                              b
10                              c

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Re: Syntax for setting data filter that excludes one of multiple categories in a field
messages.body_plain:
Hi Caroline,

Without looking at it your actual analysis I wonder, are you sure you are not looking at the 3 sets of distances that distance outputs by default for an analysis of ungrouped (i.e. exact) distances? If that is the case then note that corresponds to a single analysis and the different histograms are there just for illustration purposes, and the only difference is in the GOF measures (as the chi-squared is calculated with 3 different sets of bins). It's a coincidence you had 3 types and 3 outputs.

Please correct me if I'm wrong though. One way or the other, lets do it off the list because (1) I don't want to be wrong in front of everyone else ;) and (2) let's avoid filling other people e-mail boxes with stuff that might not be relevant. If useful to others, we'll post a summary once we have sorted what was going on.

cheers,

T

messages.body_plain:
Hi Len and others: thanks for the help with framing the query! Very helpful.

I also wanted to share what Eric explained to me in regards to my other question: why do I see three sets of results when I analyze ungrouped data? I had previously conducted analyses on only grouped data, and so was accustomed to seeing just one set of chi square results. This led me to think I had messed something up with the data filter and the program was analyzing different subsets of my data separately. That was not the case.  Eric and others have since pointed out that for ungrouped data, the program Distance will choose three different "guesses" or sets of experimental cutpoints with which to explore model fit. So in a single analysis, you should expect three sets of result pages corresponding to these three sets of experimental cutpoints.

See p. 105 (CDS: CDS Results details listing) for more information.

Eric et al., feel free to jump in here and add (or correct) any information!

Many thanks,
Caroline

messages.subject: Interesting MRDS results
messages.body_plain:
Hi Group-
We've noticed a strange pattern in our MRDS data from our large mammal aerial surveys.  We've completed 4 surveys (November 2013, February 2014, November 2014, and February 2015).  The November 13 and 14 population estimates are very similar to each other, which we would expect.  However, the February 14 and 15 population estimates are both higher than the November estimates, with February 14 being higher and February 15 being dramatically higher. Biologically, this makes no sense as there are no birth pulses between November and February and the only change would be less leaf cover in February.  Here in south Texas though, it is mostly open habitat. The methodology is consistent across all surveys.

I'm trying to figure out what the cause of this may be.  Should I be running the analyses differently between fall and winter surveys?  I have been using point independence throughout all models, but when I ran the February data with full independence, this bought my estimates closer to the November estimates.  This is to be expected, as there is negative bias associated with full independence.  I believe we are dealing with animal movement, but I'm not convinced that this movement differs for every species between the two seasons.  Would using full independence be suggested in this situation?

The frequency of observations in each distance bin has also been skewed during the February surveys, with very high detections at 0 and then falling drastically at the next bin (10m), instead of gradually (which is what November surveys follow).  I have tried to bin the observations differently, but this only brings population estimates down slightly.

I'm wondering if anyone has come across a problem like this or if anyone has any ideas as to why this may be happening? Does anyone have any ideas for the analyses that would account for this difference and give us more realistic population estimates?

Any thoughts would be greatly appreciated!
Thanks,
Mary Annala
